**The Whisper of the Universe**

There’s a quiet hum in the space between atoms, a song older than light. Some say it’s the echo of the Big Bang, stretching thin across the cosmos like a singer holding the last note of a ballad. Others think it’s the sound of time itself—ticking, not in seconds, but in the slow, steady pulse of dying stars.

I like to imagine that the universe is a library. Not the kind with dusty shelves and hushing librarians, but one made of dark matter and starlight, where every galaxy is a book, and every planet a page. Some pages are blank, waiting for life to scribble its messy, beautiful stories upon them. Others are already filled with tales we’ll never read—epics of civilizations that rose and fell before we even learned to look up.

We are such a tiny part of it all. A speck of consciousness on a speck of dust, hurtling through the void at speeds that would make our ancestors’ heads spin. And yet, here we are, asking questions. *Why?* *How?* *What’s next?* The universe doesn’t answer, of course. It just *is*. But the asking matters. It’s our way of reaching out, of touching the hem of the infinite and saying, *I see you. I’m here too.*

Sometimes, when I’m lying on the ground at night, staring up at a sky so full of stars it looks like someone sketched the universe with a child’s enthusiasm, I wonder: Does the cosmos ever look back? Does it feel us—the warmth of our lives, the weight of our dreams, the fleeting spark of our existence—and think, *Oh. There they are. Still trying.*

And then I remember: We *are* the universe looking back. Every atom in our bodies was forged in the heart of a star. We are made of the same stuff as supernovas and black holes. So when we wonder, when we ache, when we create or destroy or love—it’s the universe experiencing itself through us.

Maybe that’s the whispered secret in the silence between the stars. *You are not alone. You are not small. You are the way I know myself.*

Now if you’ll excuse me, I need to go stare at the sky some more. It’s talking. Can you hear it?
